title: URL shortener
brief: People paste a long web address and get back a short one. Millions of other people then tap that short link, so reading is almost everything. Keep every tap fast, and never lose a link.

clarify.q: Can a short link change after it is made?
clarify.a: No. A link never changes once created, so saved answers never go out of date and caching is safe.

clarify.q: How many people tap a link compared with people who make one?
clarify.a: About 99 taps for every 1 new link. This is a read-heavy system.
No. Click counts can arrive a few minutes late. The redirect itself must be fast.

notes: Short codes are 7 characters. Each stored link uses about 0.5 KB including its metadata (approx.).
About 20 new links a second on average (≈ 50 million a month, approx.).
One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

numbers.label: App servers for the evening peak
numbers.how: 5,000 req/s ÷ about 1,000 per server = 5. Run at least 6, and 7 or 8 so each sits near 70 percent, and turn on autoscaling: the 3 times spike needs about 15 (approx.).

numbers.label: Storage after 5 years
numbers.how: 50 million links a month × 12 × 5 years × 0.5 KB each ≈ 1.5 TB (approx.)

numbers.label: Possible 7-character codes
numbers.how: 62 letters and digits, to the power of 7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, so we will not run out (approx.)

hints: One server handles about 1,000 requests a second. At 5,000 that is 5 servers with no spare room, so plan for about 6 or more (the 3 from the intro is not enough here). What happens when a link goes viral?
A link never changes, so answers can be kept: put a cache in front of the database, and a CDN in front of everything for the spike.
Users, then CDN, then load balancer, then servers, then a cache, then a key-value store. Keep answers for an hour or longer.

editorial.summary: One tiny record per link, looked up by its code. Because links never change, almost every tap can be answered from a copy: first at the edge network near the person, then in memory, and only rarely from the database.

designs.name: Cached redirects at the edge
designs.why: The CDN answers most taps near the person, without touching your servers. A distributed cache catches the rest, so the key-value store only sees a trickle. You pay the CDN for every request, but a viral link adds almost no load to your own servers.

designs.name: Serverless at the edge
designs.why: Run the lookup in small functions near the user and keep every link in a key-value store. Fewer parts to run, but you pay for every call and the store sees more traffic.

designs.name: Servers, cache and autoscaling
designs.why: The pattern from the intro, sized by the numbers: a load balancer, about 8 servers so each runs near 60 percent at the evening peak, autoscaling for the 3 times spike, and a cache that keeps hot links off the database. No CDN, so it is the cheapest, but every tap crosses the ocean to your servers and the spike lands on them.

tradeoffs: A longer cache time means more hits and less cost. Links never change, so an hour or a day is safe here.
Collapsing misses stops a thousand people asking for the same cold link from hitting the database together.
Short random codes avoid a single counter, but you must check for clashes. A counter is simple but guessable.
Click counts go on a queue and are counted later, so they never slow the redirect.
editorial.realWorld: Public link shorteners handle tens of thousands of redirects a second at peak and store billions of links. Most taps are served from edge or memory copies (approx.).
